Saturday, 14 March 2037. The jury of the “Friedrich and Margarete” scholarship meets in the café. Members: Ludwig, Katrin, Mirko (the violinist from Dresden) and, for the first time, Elif, representing the scholarship holders. The second scholarship holder has to be chosen.
So, we have three applications. Who would like to start?
Me. In my view, the sixteen-year-old girl from Wedding is the strongest. Technically brilliant, two prizes at “Jugend musiziert”.
I agree with you as far as technique is concerned. However, she already has two scholarships. I wonder whether she really needs ours.
Can I say something quickly? I think we should take the little boy. Ben. He's eight. He played the scale at Grete's memorial.
Sorry, Elif, but he's been playing for a year. He barely knows more than scales.
Grete started with a scale too. And his family doesn't have a piano. He practises at school, twenty minutes a day, when the music room is free.
That's a strong argument. The scholarship is for children who would otherwise have no chance. That's what it said in Friedrich's letter.
If I may sum up: technically, the sixteen-year-old is ahead. But in terms of the purpose of the scholarship, everything speaks for Ben. Any objections?
No objection. I withdraw my proposal. Elif, you've convinced me.
Then it's decided. Unanimously. And Elif gives the laudatio.

The Friedrich and Margarete Scholarship was awarded for the second time, and for the first time under its new name, on Saturday, the twenty-first of March two thousand and thirty-seven, in the chamber music hall of the Pankow music school, the same hall in which Elif, two and a half years before, at ten, had played the song “Für S.” as the first scholarship holder. The hall was small, a hundred and twenty seats, and it was full. On the stage stood the music school's piano, freshly tuned, and beside it a lectern, and on the lectern, in a simple wooden frame, two photos side by side: Friedrich Mertens, nineteen sixty, with a pipe, and Margarete Hoffmann, nineteen fifty-six, at twenty, in a dress made from an old curtain.

The decision had been made a week before, in the café, at the table by the window, at a jury meeting which, as Ludwig said later, “was the best discussion I've experienced since New Year's Eve, and the only one without honey”. There had been three applications. A sixteen-year-old girl from Wedding, technically brilliant, with two prizes at “Jugend musiziert” and two scholarships. A fourteen-year-old boy from Pankow who played the cello and whose parents had a dental practice. And a little boy of eight called Ben, who had been playing the piano for a year, at school, twenty minutes a day, when the music room was free, because his family had no piano and lived in a two-room flat with five people. His application consisted of a single sheet, written by his teacher, and a drawing he had made himself: a piano with a face.

Elif was on the jury for the first time. Ludwig had insisted, “because otherwise the jury is made up only of old people who've forgotten what it's like to be eight”. She had listened in silence all through the meeting as Katrin argued for the sixteen-year-old, clearly and convincingly, like a journalist, and as Mirko, who had come specially from Dresden, politely contradicted her, arguing that someone with two scholarships doesn't need a third. Then, when it went quiet, Elif had raised her hand, as at school, and asked: “Can I say something quickly?” And then she had told them about Ben. About the scale at Grete's memorial. About the deep bow during which he had almost fallen off the stage. And about Grete's sentence on the last sheet of the Bach prelude: “For the child who comes after me. She will play better than me. That is the point of it all.”

Katrin had withdrawn her proposal. “You've convinced me”, she had said, and it was, as Ludwig remarked, the first time in thirty years that Katrin Krüger had been convinced by a child, “and it won't be the last”. The decision had been unanimous. And then Ludwig had said that Elif should give the laudatio. Elif had protested. She was twelve. She had never given a speech. She could play the piano, but not speak. Ludwig had only said: “Exactly. Who else?” And then, when Elif looked at him as if he had lost his mind: “You wrote Grete's book. You taught Elena to read. You wrote a letter that got a piano tuned. A speech is just a letter you read aloud.”

She wrote the speech over three evenings, with Ludwig at the kitchen table, who corrected nothing, and with Katrin on the phone, who corrected everything. She kept to the structure she had practised in the autumn with Elena, when it had been about Ludwig's toast for Grete's hundredth birthday: greeting, memory, tribute, wish, presentation. She cut everything that sounded like bureaucratic German and everything that was too sad, because Grete hadn't wanted sad services. And in the end the speech was two minutes long, “a hundred and twenty seconds”, as Elif measured with Leo's stopwatch, “one second for each seat in the hall”. She didn't learn it by heart. She just wrote five keywords on an index card, as for Elena's oral exam, and put it in the pocket of her red dress, the dress she had worn at Grete's memorial.

Hotte prepared in his own way. He had read, as he announced in the café, “for the first time in my life a book right to the end that isn't Ludwig's”: Grete's memoirs, “Das Mädchen am Tisch”, a hundred and twenty pages, in three weeks, with a magnifying glass, because his glasses, as he claimed, he had “mislaid” in nineteen ninety. He had made notes in the margin, in pencil, like Grete in her sheet music, and when Elif later saw the book, she found next to the chapter about the cellar in Wedding a single sentence in Hotte's crooked handwriting: “I was in one of them cellars too. Lichtenberg, April forty-five. I was two months old. Mum told me. Nobody played the piano. She sang. Very quiet. Till I fell asleep. Shame I've forgotten the song.” Elif didn't show it to anyone. But on the evening before the ceremony, after the speech, she practised Mr Wendland's little piece for another half hour. For all those nobody had played for.

Hotte himself said nothing about it. But on the day of the ceremony he sat in the third row, in his best tram driver's uniform, freshly ironed by Lena, and when Elif walked past him after the speech, he held her by the sleeve and whispered: “Play that Wendland piece. Afterwards. For me.” Elif nodded. And she played it, at the end, as an encore, sixteen bars, and Hotte sat completely still, with his eyes closed, like Grete.

On Saturday at three she stood at the lectern. Ben sat in the front row, between his mother and his grandmother, in a white shirt that was too big for him, and with a face as if he wanted to run away immediately. Elif looked at him and thought of Yusuf in the exam room, of the white knuckles. She smiled at him. Then she began. “Dear Ben, dear Ben's family, dear guests”, she said, and her voice trembled only on the first word. “It is a great honour for me to present this scholarship today. I received it myself two and a half years ago, when I was ten. I was afraid then that I didn't deserve it. Mrs Hoffmann told me: you don't deserve it. You get it so that one day you can pass it on.”

Then she told them about the scale. About the day in November when a little boy of eight, at a memorial where nobody was allowed to wear black, had climbed onto a stage and played a scale of C major, up and down, without a mistake, and afterwards had bowed so deeply that he almost fell. “A gentleman in the audience”, said Elif, looking towards the third row, where Hotte sat in his tram driver's uniform, “shouted then: Grete started with a scale too. It's true. I found it in her sheet music. Her first scale, nineteen forty-three, written in pencil by her teacher. She didn't have a piano at home then either. She practised on the kitchen table.” Elif paused. “The jury”, she said then, “decided unanimously in your favour, Ben. Not because you already play well. But because you've started.”

Then she handed him the certificate, in a red envelope, and with it something that wasn't in the programme: a yellowed sheet in a clear plastic sleeve. It was Grete's first scale, from nineteen forty-three, in Mr Wendland's fine pencil handwriting. “This isn't from the jury”, said Elif. “It's from Grete. She wrote that I shouldn't play all the sheet music, only the good ones. This is the best one. It's for you.” Ben took the sheet with both hands, as if it were made of glass, and looked at it for a long time. Then he did something nobody expected. He went to the piano, sat down, put the sheet on the music stand and played the scale. C major. Up and down. Without a mistake. And afterwards he bowed, carefully this time, so as not to fall off the stage.

In Sibiu, Elena sat in front of the laptop, in the kitchen, and watched the ceremony on the music school's live stream, with Dan beside her, who didn't understand a word and still clapped at every round of applause. Two weeks before she had started a C1 course, online, on Tuesdays and Thursdays, and the thirteenth notebook already had forty pages. When Elif gave her speech, Elena took notes, not every word, only the important ones, as Elif had taught her. And when Ben played the scale, Dan put his hand on her arm and said, in German, for the first time without anyone asking him: “Der Junge. Gut.” Elena wrote that in her notebook, with the date, under page six of Dan's old exercise book, which by now she kept with her in the kitchen. Page seven.

The applause went on for a long time, and Ben stood by the piano not knowing what to do with his hands. Then his mother came up onto the stage, a small woman in a flowered headscarf who, as Elif found out later, came from Afghanistan and had been learning German for two years, on a course run by Mrs Krause at the town hall. She hadn't prepared a speech. She stood at the lectern, looked out into the hall and said, quietly, with an accent Elif didn't know but understood: “I want to thank. The jury. Mrs Hoffmann, who I do not know. Without her, my son would have music only at school.” She searched for the words. “My special thanks go to …” She stopped. Then she looked at Elif and said, very simply: “Thank you, girl. You spoke for him.”

A week later Ben's mother brought a letter for Elif to the café, with a photo. The photo showed a kitchen table, in a small flat, with a rug on the wall and five mattresses rolled up in a corner during the day. On the table a keyboard had been drawn in white chalk, two octaves, black and white, not quite straight. In front of it sat Ben, with Grete's scale on a cardboard music stand, practising. On the back of the photo, in the neat handwriting of his teacher, because Ben couldn't write well yet, it said: “Ben says: now I can practise at home too. Without sound. But he hears it.” Elif stuck the photo in her diary, next to a photo of Grete's table from the cover of the book. Two tables. Ninety years apart.

After the ceremony, in the foyer of the music school, over juice and cake, Mirko came over to Elif. He was holding under his arm the viola on which he had played “Für S.” after the award, and he looked at her for a long time, with an expression she couldn't read. “You know”, he said at last, “in nineteen eighty-nine I lived on Kastanienallee, on the first floor, in the flat where Ludwig lived later. I wanted to become a musician and nobody believed in me. Except a woman in the building who taught piano and who once told me, when I was seventeen: you play out of tune, but you play. That's more than most people do. Then she showed me a photo, from her first concert, in a dress made from a curtain.” He smiled. “I never recognised her later, as an old lady. Only today. From the photo on the lectern.”

Elif told Ludwig on the way home, in the tram, and Ludwig was silent for a long time. Then he said: “See? She listened everywhere. To everyone. Even to the ones who never found out.” He looked out of the window, at Kastanienallee passing by, with the first green buds on the trees. “On Wednesday”, he said, “Leo drives on his own for the first time. Without Mr Schäfer. The M1, at seven in the morning, from Hackescher Markt to Pankow.” He smiled. “I'll sit at the window. In the café. And when he goes past, he'll ring the bell.” Elif asked: “Once or twice?” Ludwig thought about it. “That”, he said, “is for him to decide. He's a tram driver now. Tram drivers decide for themselves how many times they ring.”
